LanguageData.RimCourt.GuideGizmoDesc: How holding court works: where cases come from, how to rule, and what it does to the lord's name.
LanguageData.RimCourt.HoldCourtDesc: Convene an audience. The lord takes the seat, the colony gathers, and petitioners plead their cases one by one. You render each verdict.
LanguageData.RimCourt.NameLordDesc: Choose who holds court. Left alone, the seat goes to the throne's assigned owner, and failing that to whoever carries the most weight in the colony.
LanguageData.RimCourt.NameLordOnThrone: The seat stands on {0}'s throne, and that settles it. Reassign the throne to seat another, or let someone take it off him in open court.
LanguageData.RimCourt.PickLordDesc: No throne carries this seat, so it goes to whoever the colony holds highest. Assign a throne and its owner takes the seat on his own; until then, name your lord here.
LanguageData.RimCourt.PickLordThroneDesc: The seat stands on {0}'s throne, so the court would seat {0} on its own. Someone else holds it only because you or a challenge put him there; leave it to the seat and the throne takes it back.
LanguageData.RimCourt.LordByThrone: {0} holds court, by right of the throne.
LanguageData.RimCourt.PickLordAuto: Leave it to the seat ({0} as things stand)
LanguageData.RimCourt.NameHandDesc: Name a colonist to preside when the lord cannot: laid up, sick, or too young to swear anyone to anything. Without a Hand the seat falls back to weight of standing, as it always did.
LanguageData.RimCourt.PickHandDesc: The Hand takes the seat for the day whenever the lord is in no state to hold it. The verdicts are theirs, the reputation they build is the court's, and the lord gets it back the moment he can walk to the chair.
LanguageData.RimCourt.PickHandNone: The court will manage without a Hand
LanguageData.RimCourt.LordByHand: {0} holds court as the Hand, while the lord cannot.
LanguageData.RimCourt.StandingByHand: holds court as the Hand, while the lord cannot
LanguageData.RimCourt.SeatInheritedText:
{0} is dead, and named {1} heir before it happened. The title passes, and this court passes with it: {1} holds the seat now, by inheritance rather than by weight of standing.
Name the lord on the marker if the hall should answer to somebody else instead.
LanguageData.RimCourt.Shaped1:
{0} has ordered enough pain from that chair to stop minding it. He is {1} now, and the change is permanent.
He will be at ease with the harsh rulings he used to carry home, which is not the same thing as being a better lord.
LanguageData.RimCourt.Shaped2:
{0} has taken money across that chair often enough for it to become a habit rather than a decision. He is {1} now, and the change is permanent.
He will be at ease with the venal rulings he used to carry home, which is not the same thing as being a better lord.
LanguageData.RimCourt.Shaped3:
{0} has ducked enough judgements from that chair to stop expecting to be obeyed. He is {1} now, and the change is permanent.
He will be at ease with the weak rulings he used to carry home, which is not the same thing as being a better lord.
LanguageData.RimCourt.ShapedLostKind: Whatever was kind in {0} did not survive it.
LanguageData.RimCourt.Settings.ShapeLordHint: After a long run of harsh, venal or weak rulings, the lord permanently gains a trait to match. It takes a settled reputation, thirty points on the count, and a dozen verdicts from the same man, so it is rare and it is announced. It never grants a good trait: the seat corrupts, it does not ennoble. A kind lord made bloodthirsty is not kind any more.
LanguageData.RimCourt.Settings.NoDecay: A name once made is never forgotten
LanguageData.RimCourt.Settings.NoDecayHint: Reputation normally fades about three percent a day between sessions, so a court that stops sitting is slowly forgotten. Tick this and it never fades: whatever the lord has been judged to be, he stays. Openly a cheat, and there if you want it.
LanguageData.RimCourt.EpithetLine: From today the colony has a name for him, and it is in his name: {0}.
LanguageData.RimCourt.EpithetDropped: {0} is no longer called {1}. The name faded with the verdicts that earned it.
LanguageData.RimCourt.Settings.Epithets: The colony puts the name in his name
LanguageData.RimCourt.Settings.EpithetsHint: Once the court has a settled reputation, the lord's nickname carries it: Jaime the Just, Jaime the Cruel, Jaime the Greedy, Jaime the Weak. It changes when the name changes and goes when it fades. A dead lord keeps whatever he died with. Untick to keep names as they were.

LanguageData.RimCourt.StandingDecay:
A ruling can be refused. The colonist it went against may simply walk out of the hall, which costs the lord two points of weak, costs him twenty points of standing with everyone who watched, and sets no precedent, because nothing was settled. Whether it happens is mostly the lord's own name: a harsh lord is almost never defied and a weak one often is. Pride does the rest, so the abrasive, the greedy, the jealous, the volatile and the iron-willed are likelier than the kind and the meek, and a colonist with a royal title the lord does not have is likelier than either. Nobody walks out on a flogging, a banishment or a duel: those do not wait for consent.

The lord cannot be party to a case, but his wife, his brother and his son can. When one of them stands before the court the sheet says so in red, and ruling in their favour is not counted as just. It is counted as venal, and every other colonist takes it as what it looks like. The court draws the line at close family: spouse, lover, parent, child, sibling, grandparent. A cousin is not close enough for the hall to mutter about.

The court also remembers its own rulings. Before you rule, the sheet tells you how this court settled the last matter of the same kind, and it holds that memory for twenty days. Rule the same way and the lord gains a point of just: the court has a line and everyone can see where it is. Rule the opposite way and he gains two points of weak, because a court that changes its mind is a court worth arguing with. Letting a case time out sets no precedent and breaks none.

Old verdicts fade at three percent a day, so a name left alone drifts back toward nothing.
LanguageData.RimCourt.StandingNoDecay: Old verdicts do not fade: you have told the mod a name once made is never forgotten. Whatever this court has been judged to be, it stays, until enough rulings the other way take it off him.

LanguageData.RimCourt.StandingEffect3: One more case each session, and pettier ones reach him: a lord who cannot say no is asked more often. The seat is not safe either.

LanguageData.RimCourt.Guide.Title: Holding court
LanguageData.RimCourt.Guide.StartBody:
Place a lord's seat on a throne or a fine chair, from Architect, Misc. The marker slips under the furniture, so the throne stays visible. That is the whole setup.

Select the marker and the tile where petitioners will stand is outlined for you. They stand a few tiles in front, in the direction the chair faces. On bare ground, rotate the marker to choose which way the lord looks.

Stand the marker on a throne and its assigned owner holds court. The throne is the answer and the mod does not ask twice, so Name the lord greys out. Reassign the throne to seat another.

Without a throne, and most colonies never build one, the seat goes to whoever weighs most in the colony, on social standing and years. That is a hidden score, so Name the lord is where you settle it yourself. It is also how you take the seat back from a man who won it off you in open court.

Then use Hold court. The lord takes the seat, the free colonists gather round to watch, and cases are heard one at a time. The lord cannot be party to a case: he is judging it.

An audience spot is optional. Place one if you want petitioners further away, at the end of a great hall, or if the seat faces a wall.
LanguageData.RimCourt.Guide.CasesBody:
Cases are not invented. The court reads what your colonists actually remember, so what it hears is what your colony has lived through. Nothing else is added to make up the numbers.

A quiet colony therefore has little to try, and you will be told that nobody seeks the lord's justice today. That is not a fault: come back when something has happened.

Memories fade, and the graver the matter the longer the court will still hear it. Grave matters are always called before petty ones.

The court will not hear the same pair again for ten days. A matter settled is settled.

Travellers and neighbours hear of the court as well, and some of them come to it. They wait three days at the gate for an audience before giving up and walking off, which their people remember. How often anyone comes at all depends on the lord's name.
LanguageData.RimCourt.Guide.SheetBody:
When a petitioner has finished speaking, the clerk writes the case up and the sheet opens: the parties, what is claimed, and the rulings open to the lord.

Pick up the lord's seal below the sheet, then stamp the ruling you choose. Stamping a different line clears the first, so the parchment only ever shows one answer. Then press Pronounce the verdict.

The sheet can be dragged out of the way, and closed with the cross if you want to look at something first. Read the petition on the court marker opens it again, and so does clicking the letter.

Notes in the margin above the rulings are the court telling you what it already knows: how it settled the last matter of this kind, and whether either party is the lord's own blood. Read them before you stamp.

Saying nothing is also an answer. If the deadline runs out the case is thrown out, it is recorded as no answer given, and it counts against you as weakness.
LanguageData.RimCourt.Guide.VerdictsBody:
Every ruling changes what the parties think of each other and of the lord, and those opinions last for days. Some rulings do more than that: money changes hands for real, work orders change for real, and people leave the colony for real. The sheet says which is which.

A ruling can be refused. The colonist it went against may simply walk out of the hall, which costs the lord two points of weak, costs him twenty points of standing with everyone who watched, and sets no precedent, because nothing was settled. Whether it happens is mostly the lord's own name: a harsh lord is almost never defied and a weak one often is. Pride does the rest, so the abrasive, the greedy, the jealous, the volatile and the iron-willed are likelier than the kind and the meek, and a colonist with a royal title the lord does not have is likelier than either. Some rulings do not wait for consent and cannot be refused at all.

The lord cannot be party to a case, but his wife, his brother and his son can. When one of them stands before the court the sheet says so in red, and ruling in their favour is not counted as just. It is counted as venal, and every other colonist takes it as what it looks like. The court draws the line at close family: spouse, lover, parent, child, sibling, grandparent. A cousin is not close enough for the hall to mutter about.

The court also remembers its own rulings. Before you rule, the sheet tells you how this court settled the last matter of the same kind, and it holds that memory for twenty days. Rule the same way and the lord gains a point of just: the court has a line and everyone can see where it is. Rule the opposite way and he gains two points of weak, because a court that changes its mind is a court worth arguing with. Letting a case time out sets no precedent and breaks none.

Sending someone out of the colony is the easiest ruling to make and the only one that can walk back. Most exiles are never heard from again. Some are, and which ones is decided the day you send them: a fighter with a grudge is likelier to find his way back than a kind man or an old one, and nothing tells you which you have just made.

A lord who does not decide is a weak lord. That is the point.
LanguageData.RimCourt.Guide.PunishTitle: When a ruling has a body
LanguageData.RimCourt.Guide.PunishBody:
Some rulings are carried out in the hall rather than written down, and you watch them happen.

Where a whipping is ordered, you choose who holds the lash. Every candidate is listed with their skill and with what they think of the condemned, because handing the whip to the man's friend is a different scene from handing it to his enemy. You can also have it done without ceremony and pick nobody. Children are never offered the lash, and neither are prisoners or slaves.

A whipping hurts and needs tending afterwards. It does not kill.

Where the lord sends two parties to settle it with their fists, he has not ruled at all, and the colony notices that too. Whoever is left standing is held to be in the right.

Nothing physical happens off screen. If you cannot watch it, it is not in this mod.

Build a pillory post, from Architect, Misc. Some rulings can send the loser there instead of the lash. As with the lash, you choose who walks him there and ties him, or let him go alone. He stands bound in the yard for as long as you set in the options, and colonists who walk past stop to have their say, or to throw something. Some come over on purpose, on their own time, and stand there for a while: it counts as recreation, and the man's friends stay away. Nothing is hurt but his pride, and his opinion of everyone who laughed. If you rule for the post and have not built one, the lash is used instead.
LanguageData.RimCourt.Guide.ReputationBody:
Every verdict is worth two points on one of four counts: just, harsh, venal or weak. Ruling for a wronged party is just, punishing is harsh, throwing a case out is weak, taking money is venal.

The colony forms an opinion at eight points, so about four telling verdicts. The leading count gives the title, and it takes a three point lead to change its mind: one odd ruling will not undo a reputation.

The lord's standing, on the marker, has two pages. The first lays all of it out: the four counts as bars, what the current name is doing to your court, how many points would take it off him, and which colonists stand close enough to the seat to want it. The second is the register: what the court has ruled these twenty days and in which direction, so you can see the line you have been holding, and which colonists are running a tally against the lord and how close they are to bringing it. Click a face to find them.

The title is not decoration. Colonists carry a standing opinion of the lord because of it, and it decides who comes to court and how often, and what they think it is worth bringing. It reaches past the walls as well: a court known to be fair is one strangers will travel to and submit to, and a court known to be weak is one they will not.

Reputation fades about three percent a day between sessions. A court that sits often keeps its name; one that stops sitting is slowly forgotten, and can be steered again.

A lord known as weak or venal has more to lose than his reputation. Hold court often enough with that name and you will find out what. The colony also puts that name in his name: once it is settled, the lord is called the Just, the Cruel, the Greedy or the Weak wherever his name is shown, until the verdicts say otherwise.
LanguageData.RimCourt.Guide.SeatBody:
Stand the marker on a throne and its assigned owner holds court. The throne is the answer and the mod does not ask twice, so Name the lord greys out. Reassign the throne to seat another.

Without a throne, and most colonies never build one, the seat goes to whoever weighs most in the colony, on social standing and years. That is a hidden score, so Name the lord is where you settle it yourself.

The seat can change hands, and not always with your consent. Name the lord is also how you take it back.
Where the Royalty DLC is installed and the lord holds a title, the seat follows the crown: name an heir in his royalty tab and that heir takes the hall when he dies, instead of it falling to whoever weighs most that day. It is the only inheritance in the mod, and the game already tracks it.
The room the seat stands in is measured too, the way any room in the colony is measured. A court held under the open sky, or in a bare cell, is one strangers do not bother travelling to and one your own colonists find easy to walk out of. Space, floors, walls and a few good sculptures change both. The marker tells you what sort of hall you have and the lord's standing gives you the numbers.
Who sits there matters beyond prestige. A lord rules with his own temperament, and rulings that go against it cost him: the kind lord who orders a flogging, the ascetic who takes money, the iron-willed who lets a case lapse unanswered, each carries it for days afterwards. Ruling the way he would have anyway lifts him instead. A psychopath on the seat feels neither, which is its own kind of qualification.

The lord holds his seat while he can walk, think, stand the fever off and count as grown. When he cannot, a named Hand takes the seat for the day and gives it back the moment he recovers; without one, the seat falls to weight of standing as it always did. Name the Hand on the marker.
LanguageData.RimCourt.Guide.TipsBody:
The court dissolves if the colony comes under attack, if the lord is downed or has a mental break, or if you dismiss it yourself. No cooldown is applied in that case: convene again when things are calm.

A case cannot be heard if either party is downed, imprisoned, having a mental break, or drafted. Undraft your colonists before holding court.

The court watches what it ruled. Where a ruling changed something you can change back yourself, undo it inside a fortnight and the colony sees the lord's word broken, whatever the paperwork says.

Everything is in the mod settings: how long you have to rule, how many cases a session, days between sessions, and whether the sheet opens on its own.

A captured enemy can be brought before the seat as well. A guard fetches him from the cell and stands him where the petitioners stand, the sheet says what he did and what his people would pay to have him back, and the lord rules once: home, ransom, the post, or the sword. What counts as just depends on what he did, not on what you chose, so the sword for a man who killed one of yours is justice and the sword for a man who touched nobody is cruelty. Each prisoner is heard once. Beyond that one hearing, RimCourt does not touch prisoners or wardens.
